item.title: Medications in addiction recovery—a clash of science and stigma | Science
item.description: Is it useful to regard addiction as a moral failing or as a medical challenge? Drug use or alcohol binges during adolescence might be seen as a sign of deviance from society rules or weakness, but substance dependence, once established, is a health care problem. There are now treatments available to break “the chains of abject slavery [that] have wound themselves around the constitution” and to maintain an improved health status. Individual determination is sometimes sufficient, but pharmacologic and psychological support increase the likelihood of long-term improved health. A moral perspective about addiction, however, creates obstacles for people who are recovering from it and associates stigma with the mechanisms that can support recovery. If the individual in treatment is taking their medication daily, as prescribed, then is this evidence of addiction or of good adherence? In this area, even scientists sometimes struggle to apply the objectivity that they usually employ in other areas of their research.

item.title: Make plastics an explicit consideration in the High Seas Treaty | Science
item.description: The High Seas Treaty, formally known as the Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea on the Conservation and Sustainable Use of Marine Biological Diversity of Areas beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ Agreement), is set to hold its first Conference of the Parties (COP1) in January 2027 (1). The treaty’s preamble names plastic pollution among the pressures that it responds to, yet none of its four mechanisms—marine protected areas, environmental impact assessments (EIAs), capacity-building and technology transfer, and marine genetic resources management—addresses it (1). COP1 can close this gap, without taking on a new mandate, by making plastics an explicit consideration in two areas already on its agenda: incorporating it into how the clearing-house mechanism (CHM) will operate and into the mandate of the scientific and technical body (STB), which will shape the treaty’s science-based rules.
